pref.1: Several years of field observations have complicated an earlier explanation of a natural phenomenon, and researchers now describe the situation with more caution than certainty. Their report compares preliminary measurements with older assumptions and emphasizes how much the interpretation depends on incomplete but suggestive evidence gathered across different seasons and locations.
pref.2: A regional archive recently acquired letters, maps, and photographs that changed how historians understand a public project. Because the records were fragmentary, the scholars had to connect small pieces of evidence across several sources before describing the project's development, the people who shaped it, and the reasons its significance had been overlooked.
pref.3: At a community arts center, a curator prepared an exhibition about creators whose work drew on scientific observation, local history, and collaboration. The exhibition notes explain how individual decisions, materials, audiences, and institutional settings shaped the meaning of each work over time rather than treating the finished objects as isolated achievements.
pref.4: A city planning report compares several approaches to improving transportation, public health, and access to shared spaces. The report links individual examples to broader patterns, showing how policy choices can produce effects that are gradual, indirect, or difficult to measure immediately, especially when different neighborhoods experience the same policy in different ways.
pref.5: In a laboratory study, researchers tracked a process over multiple stages and found that the outcome depended on timing, environment, and the interaction of several variables. Their summary presents the evidence carefully because a small change in wording would alter the precision of the claim and might make the conclusion sound broader than the data support.

The following text is adapted from Indian Boyhood, a 1902 memoir by Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman), a Santee Dakota writer. In the text, Ohiyesa recalls how the women in his tribe harvested maple syrup during his childhood.

Now the women began to test the trees - moving leisurely among them, axe in hand, and striking a single quick blow, to see if the sap would appear. The trees, like people, have their individual characters; some were ready to yield up their life-blood, while others were more reluctant. Now one of the birchen basins was set under each tree, and a hardwood chip driven deep into the cut which the axe had made. From the corners of this chip - at first drop by drop, then more freely - the sap trickled into the little dishes.

o10.body:
Text 1
Ecologists have long wondered how thousands of microscopic phytoplankton species can live together near ocean surfaces competing for the same resources. According to conventional wisdom, one species should emerge after outcompeting the rest. So why do so many species remain? Ecologists' many efforts to explain this phenomenon still haven't uncovered a satisfactory explanation.

Text 2
Ecologist Michael Behrenfeld and colleagues have connected phytoplankton's diversity to their microscopic size. Because these organisms are so tiny, they are spaced relatively far apart from each other in ocean water and, moreover, experience that water as a relatively dense substance. This in turn makes it hard for them to move around and interact with one another. Therefore, says Behrenfeld's team, direct competition among phytoplankton probably happens much less than previously thought.

Based on the texts, how would Behrenfeld and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the "conventional wisdom" discussed in Text 1?

opts.A: By arguing that it is based on a misconception about phytoplankton species competing with one another
opts.B: By asserting that it fails to recognize that routine replenishment of ocean nutrients prevents competition between phytoplankton species
opts.C: By suggesting that their own findings help clarify how phytoplankton species are able to compete with larger organisms
opts.D: By recommending that more ecologists focus their research on how competition among phytoplankton species is increased with water density

o11.body:
In 2014, Amelia Quon and her team at NASA set out to build a helicopter capable of flying on Mars. Because Mars's atmosphere is only one percent as dense as Earth's, the air of Mars would not provide enough resistance to the rotating blades of a standard helicopter for the aircraft to stay aloft. For five years, Quon's team tested designs in a lab that mimicked Mars's atmospheric conditions. The craft the team ultimately designed can fly on Mars because its blades are longer and rotate faster than those of a helicopter of the same size built for Earth.

According to the text, why would a helicopter built for Earth be unable to fly on Mars?

opts.A: Because Mars and Earth have different atmospheric conditions
opts.B: Because the blades of helicopters built for Earth are too large to work on Mars
opts.C: Because the gravity of Mars is much weaker than the gravity of Earth
opts.D: Because helicopters built for Earth are too small to handle the conditions on Mars

o13.body: In 1934 physicist Eugene Wigner posited the existence of a crystal consisting entirely of electrons in a honeycomb-like structure. The so-called Wigner crystal remained largely conjecture, however, until Feng Wang and colleagues announced in 2021 that they had captured an image of one. The researchers trapped electrons between two semiconductors and then cooled the apparatus, causing the electrons to settle into a crystalline structure. By inserting an ultrathin sheet of graphene above the crystal, the researchers obtained an impression - the first visual confirmation of the Wigner crystal.

opts.A: Researchers have obtained the most definitive evidence to date of the existence of the Wigner crystal.
opts.B: Researchers have identified an innovative new method for working with unusual crystalline structures.
opts.C: Graphene is the most important of the components required to capture an image of a Wigner crystal.
opts.D: It's difficult to acquire an image of a Wigner crystal because of the crystal's honeycomb structure.

o15.body:
When digging for clams, their primary food, sea otters damage the roots of eelgrass plants growing on the seafloor. Near Vancouver Island in Canada, the otter population is large and well established, yet the eelgrass meadows are healthier than those found elsewhere off Canada's coast. To explain this, conservation scientist Erin Foster and colleagues compared the Vancouver Island meadows to meadows where otters are absent or were reintroduced only recently. Finding that the Vancouver Island meadows have a more diverse gene pool than the others do, Foster hypothesized that damage to eelgrass roots increases the plant's rate of sexual reproduction; this, in turn, boosts genetic diversity, which benefits the meadow's health overall.

Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine Foster's hypothesis?

opts.A: At some sites in the study, eelgrass meadows are found near otter populations that are small and have only recently been reintroduced.
opts.B: At several sites not included in the study, there are large, well-established sea otter populations but no eelgrass meadows.
opts.C: At several sites not included in the study, eelgrass meadows' health correlates negatively with the length of residence and size of otter populations.
opts.D: At some sites in the study, the health of plants unrelated to eelgrass correlates negatively with the length of residence and size of otter populations.

o29.body:
While researching a topic, a student has taken notes about NASA rovers and microprobes. The notes say that NASA uses wheeled rovers to explore Mars, but rovers cannot explore regions inaccessible to wheeled vehicles and are heavy, making them difficult to land. Microprobes, robotic probes weighing as little as 50 milligrams, could be deployed virtually anywhere on Mars and have been proposed as an alternative to rovers.

The student wants to explain an advantage of microprobes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

opts.A: Despite being heavy, NASA's rovers can land successfully on the surface of Mars.
opts.B: Microprobes, which weigh as little as 50 milligrams, could explore areas of Mars that are inaccessible to NASA's heavy, wheeled rovers.
opts.C: NASA currently uses its rovers on Mars, but microprobes have been proposed as an alternative.
opts.D: Though they are different sizes, both microprobes and rovers can be used to explore the surface of Mars.

o33.body:
While researching a topic, a student has taken notes about Beatles songwriting credits. British musicians John Lennon and Paul McCartney shared writing credit for numerous Beatles songs, though many Lennon-McCartney songs were actually written by either Lennon or McCartney, not both. The exact authorship of specific parts of many Beatles songs, such as the verse for "In My Life," is disputed. Mark Glickman, Jason Brown, and Ryan Song used statistical methods to analyze the musical content of Beatles songs and concluded that there is an 18.9% probability that McCartney wrote the verse for "In My Life," stating that the verse is "consistent with Lennon's songwriting style."

The student wants to make a generalization about the kind of study conducted by Glickman, Brown, and Song. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

opts.A: Based on statistical analysis, Glickman, Brown, and Song claim that John Lennon wrote the verse of "In My Life."
opts.B: There is only an 18.9% probability that Paul McCartney wrote the verse for "In My Life"; John Lennon is the more likely author.
opts.C: It is likely that John Lennon, not Paul McCartney, wrote the verse for "In My Life."
opts.D: Researchers have used statistical methods to address questions of authorship within the field of music.
